papers.title: Applied Statistics
papers.instructions: Time: 3 hours. Candidates may attempt ALL questions in Section A and at most TWO questions in Section B. Each question should start on a fresh page.

items.label: A1
items.text: State and explain any four measurement scales in non-parametric statistics.
items.model:
Nominal: categories with no natural order (e.g. gender, province, car make). Only counts and the mode make sense.
Ordinal: categories that can be ranked but the gaps are not equal (e.g. Likert ratings, grades, class position). Medians and rank-based tests apply.
Interval: equal gaps but no true zero (e.g. temperature in °C, calendar year). Differences are meaningful, ratios are not.
Ratio: equal gaps and a true zero (e.g. height, income, time, number of defects). Ratios are meaningful.
items.teach: Name the four scales in order of strength, then give one example of each.

items.label: A2(a)
items.text: Define: Null hypothesis
items.model: The null hypothesis (H0) is the statement of no effect or no difference that is assumed true until the data give enough evidence against it, e.g. H0: μ1 = μ2. The test either rejects H0 or fails to reject it.

items.label: A2(b)
items.text: Define: Significance level
items.model: The significance level (α) is the probability of rejecting H0 when it is actually true (a Type I error). It is fixed before the test, commonly 0.05 or 0.01, and sets the size of the critical region.

items.label: A2(c)
items.text: Define: Test statistic
items.model: A test statistic is a value calculated from the sample data (e.g. z, t, χ², U) that is compared with a critical value or used to find a p-value in order to decide whether to reject H0.

items.label: A2(d)
items.text: Define: Skewness
items.model: Skewness measures the asymmetry of a distribution about its centre. Positive skew has a long right tail (mean > median); negative skew has a long left tail (mean < median); zero means symmetric.

items.label: A3
items.text:
The table shows departures from normal daily temperatures recorded in Harare in 2019.
Days 1–15: 12, 13, 12, 11, 5, 2, −1, 2, −1, 3, 2, −6, −7, −7, −12
Days 16–30: −9, 6, 7, 10, 10, 1, 1, 3, 7, −2, −6, −6, −5, −2, −2
We would like to know whether we may conclude that the pattern of departures above and below the normal is the result of a non-random process.
items.model:
Runs test on the signs of the departures.
H0: the sequence of + and − departures is random. H1: it is not random.
Signs: + + + + + + − + − + + − − − − − + + + + + + + + − − − − − −
n1 (above normal) = 17, n2 (below normal) = 13, N = 30, number of runs R = 8.
μR = 2n1n2/N + 1 = 15.733;  σR = √[2n1n2(2n1n2 − N) / (N²(N−1))] = 2.641.
Z = (R − μR)/σR = (8 − 15.733)/2.641 = -2.928.
Critical value at 5% (two-tailed) = ±1.96. Since |-2.928| > 1.96, reject H0.
Conclusion: there are too few runs, so the departures are not random. They cluster in warm and cold spells.
items.teach: Count a run each time the sign changes. Use the normal approximation because n1 and n2 are large.

items.label: A4(a)
items.text:
Two independent random samples were selected from normal populations.
Sample 1: 13, 3, 8, 5, 6, 7, 4, 9, 10, 9 (n = 10)
Sample 2: 14, 7, 7, 9, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 (n = 11)
Calculate Sp², the pooled estimator of σ².

items.label: A4(b)
items.text: Test at the 5% significance level whether the two populations are the same.
items.model:
H0: μ1 = μ2 against H1: μ1 ≠ μ2 (equal variances assumed).
t = (x̄1 − x̄2)/√[Sp²(1/n1 + 1/n2)] = (7.400 − 9.545)/√[8.375(1/10 + 1/11)] = -1.697.
Degrees of freedom = 19. Critical value t0.025,19 = ±2.093.
Since |-1.697| < 2.093 we fail to reject H0.
Conclusion: no significant difference between the two populations at the 5% level.

items.label: B5(a)
items.text:
The effectiveness of advertising for two rival coffee brands was compared. Participants rated the likelihood of buying (out of 10). Half rated Brand X, the other half Brand Y.
Brand X ratings (participants 1–6): 3, 4, 2, 6, 2, 5
Brand Y ratings (participants 1–6): 9, 7, 5, 10, 6, 8
Is there a significant difference between the ratings given to each brand? (Use the Mann-Whitney test)
items.model:
H0: the two brands have the same distribution of ratings. H1: they differ (two-tailed, α = 0.05).
Rank all 12 values together (ties get the average rank):
Brand X ranks: 3, 4, 1.5, 7.5, 1.5, 5.5 → ΣR = 23
Brand Y ranks: 11, 9, 5.5, 12, 7.5, 10 → ΣR = 55
U = n1n2 + n2(n2+1)/2 − ΣR:  U1 = 36 + 21 − 23 = 34,  U2 = 36 + 21 − 55 = 2.
Test statistic U = smaller value = 2.
Critical value (two-tailed, α = 0.05, n1 = n2 = 6) = 5. Reject H0 if U ≤ 5.
Since 2 ≤ 5, reject H0.
Conclusion: there is a significant difference. Brand Y was rated higher, so its advert is more effective.
items.teach: Rank the combined data, sum ranks for one brand, apply the booklet formula, and compare the smaller U with the table.
items.sec: SECTION B (60 marks, attempt TWO questions)

items.label: B5(b)
items.text: Outline the main steps of hypothesis testing.
items.model:
1. State H0 and H1.
2. Choose the significance level α.
3. Choose the appropriate test and state its assumptions.
4. Calculate the test statistic from the sample.
5. Find the critical value (or p-value) and define the critical region.
6. Decision: reject H0 if the statistic falls in the critical region; otherwise fail to reject.
7. State the conclusion in the context of the problem.

items.label: B5(c)(i)
items.text:
10 patients were taken at random to assess blood pressure before and after oral contraception. Before (X): 4.61, 6.42, 5.4, 4.54, 3.98, 3.82, 5.01, 4.34, 3.8. After (Y): 3.84, 5.57, 5.85, 4.80, 3.68, 2.96, 4.41, 4.34, 3.8.
Is this a matched pair or not? Explain.
items.model: Yes, it is a matched (paired) design. Each X and Y value is measured on the same patient, so the two observations in each pair are dependent. The analysis must use the differences d = X − Y, not two independent samples.

items.label: B5(c)(ii)
items.text: Is there significant difference between blood pressure before (X) and after (Y) oral contraception?
items.model:
Differences d = X − Y: 0.77, 0.85, -0.45, -0.26, 0.30, 0.86, 0.60, 0.00, 0.00.
H0: μd = 0, H1: μd ≠ 0 (α = 0.05).
d̄ = 0.2967, sd = 0.4979, n = 9 pairs.
t = d̄√n / sd = 0.2967×3/0.4979 = 1.788.
Critical value t0.025,8 = ±2.306.
Since 1.788 < 2.306, fail to reject H0.
Conclusion: no significant difference in blood pressure before and after oral contraception.
items.teach: Paired t-test: d̄√n / sd with n − 1 = 8 degrees of freedom. (The booklet says 10 patients but only 9 pairs are listed.)

items.label: B6(a)
items.text:
Students rated a sentence for acceptability (0 = totally unacceptable, 5 = totally acceptable) in informal spoken and formal written English. The investigator predicts informal spoken will be judged more acceptable.
Subjects 1–15, (informal, formal): (5,5) (4,2) (5,3) (4,4) (3,1) (2,3) (4,3) (5,1) (4,2) (2,3) (4,2) (4,3) (5,3) (3,5) (3,0)
Is there a significant difference between the two sets of scores? Apply the sign test.
items.model:
Differences (informal − formal): 0, +, +, 0, +, −, +, +, +, −, +, +, +, −, +.
Two ties (subjects 1 and 4) are dropped, so n = 13. Plus signs = 10, minus signs = 3. Test value = smaller count = 3.
H0: no difference. H1: informal is rated higher (one-tailed, the investigator's prediction), α = 0.05.
Sign-test table, n = 13, one-tailed α = 0.05: critical value = 3. Since 3 ≤ 3, reject H0: informal spoken English is rated significantly more acceptable.
If a two-tailed test is used (α = 0.05, critical value 2), 3 > 2 and H0 is not rejected. State which form the question intends.
items.teach: Drop zero differences, count + and −, use the smaller count against the table.

items.label: B6(b)(i)
items.text: Let X be a random sample from a Poisson distribution with parameter μ. Test H0: μ = 2 against H1: μ = 3 using the decision: reject H0 if X > 2. Calculate the probability of a Type I error.

items.label: B6(b)(ii)
items.text: Calculate the probability of a Type II error.

items.label: B6(b)(iii)
items.text: Calculate the power of the test.

items.label: B6(c)
items.text: Let 30, 22, 32, 26, 24, 40, 34, 36, 32, 33, 28, 30 be a realisation from a certain population. Calculate the coefficient of skewness and comment on the result.
items.model:
n = 12, mean = 30.583, median = 31, s = 5.089.
Pearson's coefficient = 3(mean − median)/s = 3(30.583 − 31)/5.089 = -0.246.
The value is close to 0 and slightly negative, so the data are approximately symmetric with a very slight left skew. (The moment coefficient is 0.016, also essentially 0.)

items.label: B6(d)
items.text: Econometric data assess the effects of dollarization (x1) and inflation (x2) on economic growth (y). The fitted model is y = 100 + 0.5x1 − 7.6x2. Comment on the model.
items.model:
• Intercept 100: predicted growth when x1 = x2 = 0.
• Slope 0.5: holding inflation constant, a one-unit rise in dollarization raises growth by 0.5 units on average.
• Slope −7.6: holding dollarization constant, a one-unit rise in inflation lowers growth by 7.6 units, so inflation is the far stronger influence and its effect is harmful.
• The model is only useful once checked: significance of each coefficient (t-tests), overall fit (R², F-test), residual diagnostics and multicollinearity between x1 and x2.

items.label: B7(a)
items.text:
A random sample of invoices from a chain of book shops gives:
            Novel  Textbook  General Interest
Hardback      3       16          2
Paperback     4        2          3
Assess at the 5% level whether there is an association between the type of book sold and its cover.
items.model:
H0: type of book and cover are independent. H1: they are associated.
Row totals 21 and 9; column totals 7, 18, 5; N = 30.
Expected = row × column / N:  Hardback 4.9, 12.6, 3.5;  Paperback 2.1, 5.4, 1.5.
χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 7.657.
df = (2−1)(3−1) = 2. Critical χ²0.05,2 = 5.991.
Since 7.657 > 5.991, reject H0: there is an association. Hardback books are mostly textbooks, paperbacks are mostly novels or general interest.
Caution: four of six expected counts are below 5, so the approximation is weak. Combine categories or use an exact test to confirm.
items.teach: Find expected counts from totals, sum (O − E)²/E, compare with the chi-square table at df = 2.

items.label: B7(b)
items.text:
8 people took part in a study of whether exercise alleviates depression. Each person was randomly allocated to one of three groups, then rated how depressed they felt (Likert 1–100) after a month.
No exercise: 23, 26, 51, 49, 58, 37, 29, 44
20 minutes jogging: 22, 27, 39, 29, 46, 48, 49, 65
60 minutes jogging: 59, 66, 38, 49, 56, 60, 56, 62
Use the Kruskal-Wallis test to test if physical exercise alleviates depression.
items.model:
H0: the three groups have the same distribution of ratings. H1: at least one group differs. α = 0.05.
Rank all 24 values together (ties averaged). Rank sums: no exercise R1 = 76.5, 20 min R2 = 79.5, 60 min R3 = 144 (total 300).
H = 12/[n(n+1)] Σ(Ri²/ni) − 3(n+1) = 12/(24×25) × (76.5²/8 + 79.5²/8 + 144²/8) − 75 = 7.271.
df = k − 1 = 2. Critical χ²0.05,2 = 5.991.
Since 7.271 > 5.991, reject H0: the groups differ significantly.
Note the direction: the 60-minute group has the highest ratings. If a higher rating means more depressed, the data do not show that exercise alleviates depression. Always check how the scale is defined.

items.label: B7(c)(i)
items.text: Define: test statistics.
items.model: A test statistic is a quantity computed from sample data under the assumption that H0 is true. Its sampling distribution is known, so comparing it with a critical value (or finding its p-value) lets us decide whether the data are consistent with H0. Examples: z, t, χ², U, H.

items.label: B7(c)(ii)
items.text: Define: run, as used in the runs test.
items.model: A run is an unbroken sequence of identical symbols (for example + + + or − −) in an ordered series, bounded by a different symbol or by the end of the series. The runs test uses the total number of runs to judge whether the order of the data is random. For example, ++−−−+ has 3 runs.

papers.title: Applied Statistics Assignment
papers.instructions: Level 2 Applied Statistics Assignment. Answer ALL questions in Section A and Section B. Show all working. Give numerical answers to 4 decimal places unless stated. Statistical tables may be used.

items.label: A1(a)
items.text:
The number of hours spent studying by 12 students before an examination: 5, 8, 6, 9, 7, 8, 4, 11, 7, 6, 7, 10.
Calculate the mean, median and mode of the data.
items.model:
Sum = 88, n = 12.
Mean = 88/12 = 7.3333.
Ordered data: 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 7, 7, 8, 8, 9, 10, 11. Median = (6th + 7th)/2 = (7 + 7)/2 = 7.
Mode = 7 (appears three times).

items.label: A1(b)
items.text: Calculate the range, variance and standard deviation.
items.model:
Range = 11 − 4 = 7.
Σx² = 690. Sample variance s² = [Σx² − n·x̄²]/(n−1) = 4.0606.
Standard deviation s = √4.0606 = 2.0151.
(Population variance, dividing by n, would be 3.7222.)

items.label: A1(c)
items.text: Determine the first and third quartiles and hence calculate the interquartile range.
items.model:
Using position (n+1)p: Q1 is at position 3.25, giving 6 + 0.25(6 − 6) = 6.
Q3 is at position 9.75, giving 8 + 0.75(9 − 8) = 8.75.
IQR = 8.75 − 6 = 2.75.
(Median-of-halves method gives Q1 = 6, Q3 = 8.5, IQR = 2.5. State which method you use.)

items.label: A2(a)
items.text:
Three components A, B, C fail independently with P(A) = 0.08, P(B) = 0.15, P(C) = 0.22.
Find the probability that none of the three components fails.

items.label: A2(b)
items.text: Find the probability that at least one component fails.
items.model: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none) = 1 − 0.6100 = 0.3900.

items.label: A2(c)
items.text: Find the probability that exactly two components fail.

items.label: A2(d)
items.text: A student is selected at random. P(uses statistical software) = 0.65, P(completed the assignment) = 0.70, P(both) = 0.52. Find P(completed the assignment | uses software).

items.label: A3(a)
items.text: The lifetime X (hours) of an electronic component is normal with mean 520 and standard deviation 45. Find P(X > 590).

items.label: A3(c)
items.text: Determine the lifetime corresponding to the 90th percentile.

items.label: A3(d)
items.text: State two properties of the normal distribution.
items.model:
1. It is symmetric and bell-shaped about the mean, so mean = median = mode.
2. About 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values lie within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean. (Also: total area = 1, completely described by μ and σ.)

items.label: A4(a)
items.text: Explain the distinction between descriptive and inferential statistics, giving one practical example of each.
items.model:
Descriptive statistics summarise and present the data actually collected (means, tables, charts). Example: the average mark of a class of 40 students.
Inferential statistics use a sample to draw conclusions about a population, with a measure of uncertainty (estimation, hypothesis tests). Example: using 100 sampled students to estimate the mean mark of all students at the university.

items.label: A4(b)(i)
items.text: Define: Null hypothesis
items.model: The statement of no effect or no difference that is tested and assumed true unless the data give strong evidence against it.

items.label: A4(b)(ii)
items.text: Define: Significance level
items.model: The probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis (Type I error), chosen in advance, e.g. 0.05.

items.label: A4(b)(iii)
items.text: Define: Test statistic
items.model: A function of the sample data, with known distribution under H0, used to decide whether to reject H0.

items.label: A4(c)(i)
items.text: Explain what is meant by an outlier (a dataset has one observation substantially larger than the others).
items.model: An outlier is an observation that lies unusually far from the bulk of the data, for example beyond Q3 + 1.5 × IQR or more than 3 standard deviations from the mean.

items.label: A4(c)(ii)
items.text: State one measure of central tendency that is resistant to outliers and explain why.
items.model: The median. It depends only on the middle position of the ordered data, so an extreme value changes the median very little, while it pulls the mean strongly.

items.label: A4(d)
items.text: Briefly explain the Central Limit Theorem and state one reason why it is important in inference.
items.model: For a large sample, the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal with mean μ and standard deviation σ/√n, whatever the shape of the population. It matters because it justifies using z and t procedures (confidence intervals and tests) even when the population is not normal.

items.label: B5(a)
items.text:
A random sample of 64 computer science students has a mean examination score of 66. The population standard deviation is 12.
Construct a 95% confidence interval for the population mean.

items.label: B5(b)
items.text: Determine the minimum sample size required to estimate the population mean to within 2.5 marks with 95% confidence.

items.label: B5(c)
items.text: In a random sample of 450 students, 270 use statistical software regularly. Obtain a point estimate of the population proportion.

items.label: B5(d)
items.text: Construct a 95% confidence interval for the population proportion.

items.label: B5(e)
items.text: Determine the sample size required to estimate the proportion to within 0.03 with 95% confidence, using p = 0.5.

items.label: B5(f)
items.text: State two factors that affect the width of a confidence interval.
items.model:
1. Confidence level: higher confidence gives a wider interval.
2. Sample size: larger n gives a narrower interval. (Also the variability σ or s: more variability gives a wider interval.)

items.label: B5(g)
items.text: Briefly explain the meaning of a 95% confidence interval.
items.model: If we took many random samples and built an interval from each in the same way, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true population parameter. It does not mean there is a 95% probability that the parameter lies in one particular computed interval. The parameter is fixed, the interval is random.

items.label: B5(h)
items.text: State one condition under which the normal approximation may be used for estimating a population proportion.
items.model: The sample is large enough that both np̂ ≥ 5 and n(1 − p̂) ≥ 5 (some texts use 10). Here 270 and 180 easily satisfy this. The sample must also be random.

items.label: B5(i)
items.text: Distinguish between a point estimate and an interval estimate.
items.model: A point estimate is a single number computed from the sample as the best guess of a parameter (e.g. x̄ = 66). An interval estimate gives a range of plausible values with a stated confidence level (e.g. 63.06 to 68.94). The interval shows the precision of the estimate, which a point estimate does not.

items.label: B6(a)
items.text:
A manufacturer claims the mean battery lifetime is 52 hours. A random sample of 18 batteries gives a sample mean of 49.6 hours and standard deviation 4.8 hours.
State the null and alternative hypotheses for testing whether the mean differs from 52 hours.
items.model:
H0: μ = 52 hours.
H1: μ ≠ 52 hours (two-tailed).

items.label: B6(b)
items.text: Perform an appropriate hypothesis test at the 5% significance level. State the test statistic, critical value and conclusion.
items.model:
σ unknown and n is small, so use a one-sample t-test.
t = (x̄ − μ0)/(s/√n) = (49.6 − 52)/(4.8/√18) = −2.4/1.1314 = -2.121.
df = 17. Critical values t0.025,17 = ±2.110.
Since |-2.121| = 2.121 > 2.110, reject H0.
Conclusion: at the 5% level the mean lifetime differs significantly from 52 hours (it is lower). The result is marginal.

items.label: B6(c)
items.text: Construct a 95% confidence interval for the population mean battery lifetime.
items.model:
49.6 ± 2.110(4.8/√18) = 49.6 ± 2.3872.
95% CI: (47.21, 51.99). The value 52 lies just outside, consistent with rejecting H0.

items.label: B6(d)
items.text: Two independent computer systems: System A n = 12, x̄ = 41.8, s = 5.4; System B n = 15, x̄ = 46.9, s = 6.3. Assuming normal populations with equal variances, test at 5% whether the two population means differ.
items.model:
H0: μA = μB, H1: μA ≠ μB.
Sp² = [11(5.4²) + 14(6.3²)]/25 = 35.057.
t = (41.8 − 46.9)/√[35.057(1/12 + 1/15)] = −5.1/2.2931 = -2.224.
df = 25. Critical value = ±2.060.
Since |-2.224| > 2.060, reject H0: the mean processing times differ significantly (System A is faster).

items.label: B6(e)
items.text: Explain the difference between a Type I error and a Type II error.
items.model:
Type I error: rejecting H0 when H0 is true (a false alarm). Its probability is α.
Type II error: failing to reject H0 when H0 is false (a missed effect). Its probability is β, and power = 1 − β.
Reducing one kind of error generally increases the other for a fixed sample size.

items.label: B6(f)
items.text: State the meaning of the level of significance of a statistical test.
items.model: It is the maximum probability of a Type I error that we are willing to accept, P(reject H0 | H0 true) = α. It fixes the size of the critical region.

items.label: B6(g)
items.text: Outline the main steps involved in carrying out a hypothesis test.
items.model:
1. State H0 and H1.
2. Choose α.
3. Select the test and check assumptions.
4. Compute the test statistic.
5. Find the critical value or p-value.
6. Decide: reject or fail to reject H0.
7. Conclude in the context of the problem.

items.label: B7(a)
items.text:
Hours studied X and examination mark Y for eight students.
X: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9
Y: 46, 51, 55, 60, 66, 69, 75, 78
Calculate the Pearson correlation coefficient r and interpret its value.
items.model:
Sxx = 42, Syy = 918.000, Sxy = 196.
r = Sxy/√(Sxx·Syy) = 0.9982.
Interpretation: a very strong positive linear relationship. More study hours go with higher marks.
items.teach: Compute x̄ = 5.5, ȳ = 62.5 first, then the three sums of squares.

items.label: B7(b)
items.text: Determine the least-squares estimates of β0 and β1 and write the fitted regression equation.

items.label: B7(c)
items.text: Calculate the coefficient of determination R² and interpret the result.
items.model: R² = r² = 0.9964. About 99.64% of the variation in examination marks is explained by hours studied.

items.label: B7(d)
items.text: Test, at the 5% significance level, whether there is a significant linear relationship between study time and examination mark.
items.model:
H0: β1 = 0, H1: β1 ≠ 0.
t = β̂1/SE(β̂1) = 4.6667/0.1150 = 40.576.
df = 6. Critical value t0.025,6 = ±2.447.
Since 40.58 > 2.447, reject H0: there is a significant linear relationship.

items.label: B7(e)
items.text: Estimate the examination mark for a student who studies for 5.5 hours.

items.label: B7(f)
items.text: State two assumptions that should be checked before using the fitted regression for prediction.
items.model:
1. Linearity: the mean of Y changes linearly with X (check the scatter plot and residual plot).
2. Independence of the errors.
3. Constant variance (homoscedasticity) of the errors.
4. Normally distributed errors (check with a residual histogram or Q-Q plot).

items.label: B7(g)
items.text: Briefly explain why a scatter plot should be constructed before fitting a simple linear regression model.
items.model: A scatter plot shows whether the relationship is roughly linear, reveals outliers or influential points, and shows unequal spread. These are things r and the fitted line cannot reveal. A curved pattern would make a straight-line model inappropriate.

items.label: B7(h)
items.text: State one limitation of using correlation as a measure of association.
items.model: Correlation measures only the strength of a linear relationship. A strong non-linear relationship can give r near 0. It is also sensitive to outliers and does not show causation. A high r does not mean X causes Y.

papers.title: Applied Statistics 1
papers.instructions: Time: 3 hours. Candidates may attempt any THREE questions. Each question should start on a fresh page.

items.label: 1(a)
items.text: State the four measurement scales giving an example of each.
items.model:
Nominal: categories with no natural order (e.g. gender, province, car make). Only counts and the mode make sense.
Ordinal: categories that can be ranked but the gaps are not equal (e.g. Likert ratings, grades, class position). Medians and rank-based tests apply.
Interval: equal gaps but no true zero (e.g. temperature in °C, calendar year). Differences are meaningful, ratios are not.
Ratio: equal gaps and a true zero (e.g. height, income, time, number of defects). Ratios are meaningful.

items.label: 1(b)(i)
items.text:
Annual returns for Fund Y: Year 1: 19.5%, Year 2: −1.9%, Year 3: 19.7%, Year 4: 35.0%, Year 5: 5.7%.
Calculate the geometric mean.

items.label: 1(b)(ii)
items.text: Calculate the harmonic mean.
items.model:
Using the growth factors (1 + R): H = n/Σ(1/x) = 5/(1/1.195 + 1/0.981 + 1/1.197 + 1/1.350 + 1/1.057) = 1.1420, a return of 14.20%.
Note: the harmonic mean of the raw percentages cannot be used because the −1.9% value makes it meaningless. Always compare AM ≥ GM ≥ HM.

items.label: 1(c)
items.text:
15 patients with pre-hypertension did an exercise programme for 6 weeks. Systolic BP before and after: Patient 1: 70 → 36; Patients 2 to 15: 78 → 20 each.
Is there a difference in systolic blood pressure after the programme compared with before? Use the Wilcoxon signed ranks test.
items.model:
H0: no difference in median BP. H1: there is a difference (two-tailed, α = 0.05).
Differences (before − after): patient 1 = 34, patients 2–15 = 58 (all positive).
Rank |d|: 34 gets rank 1; the fourteen 58s share ranks 2–15, average 8.5.
W+ = 1 + 14(8.5) = 120, W− = 0. Test statistic W = smaller sum = 0.
Critical value (n = 15, two-tailed, α = 0.05) = 25. Reject H0 if W ≤ 25.
Since 0 ≤ 25, reject H0.
Conclusion: blood pressure is significantly different, and it is lower after the exercise programme.
items.teach: All differences have the same sign, so one rank sum is 0.

items.label: 2(a)
items.text: Define the term kurtosis and describe any three types of kurtosis you are familiar with. You may include diagrams.
items.model:
Kurtosis measures the peakedness of a distribution and the heaviness of its tails relative to a normal curve.
• Mesokurtic: kurtosis ≈ 3 (excess 0). Normal-like peak and tails.
• Leptokurtic: kurtosis > 3. Sharper peak and heavier tails (more extreme values).
• Platykurtic: kurtosis < 3. Flatter peak and lighter tails.

items.label: 2(b)(ii)
items.text: Evaluate the standard deviation.

items.label: 2(b)(iii)
items.text: Evaluate the coefficient of variation.

items.label: 2(b)(iv)
items.text: Evaluate the median.
items.model: n = 21, so the median is the 11th ordered value = 36.

items.label: 2(b)(v)
items.text: Evaluate q0.69.

items.label: 2(b)(vi)
items.text: Evaluate the interquartile range.

items.label: 2(b)(vii)
items.text: Determine with justification whether there are any outliers.
items.model:
Fences: Q1 − 1.5 IQR = 19.5 − 46.5 = −27; Q3 + 1.5 IQR = 50.5 + 46.5 = 97.
All values lie between −27 and 97 (the largest, 87, is below 97), so there are no outliers by the 1.5 × IQR rule. The value 87 is large but not outlying.

items.label: 2(b)(viii)
items.text: State with justification if there is any type of skew.
items.model: Pearson's coefficient = 3(mean − median)/s = 3(35.571 − 36)/19.392 = -0.066, close to 0, so the centre looks symmetric. The upper whisker (50.5 to 87) is longer than the lower (3 to 19.5), and the moment skewness is 0.69, which suggests mild positive skew caused by the value 87.

items.label: 2(b)(ix)
items.text: Draw a suitably labelled box plot.
items.model:
Five-number summary: minimum 3, Q1 19.5, median 36, Q3 50.5, maximum 87.
Draw a horizontal axis from 0 to 90. Box from 19.5 to 50.5 with a line at 36. Whiskers from 3 to 19.5 and from 50.5 to 87 (no outliers). Label the axis (values) and mark the five numbers.

items.label: 3(a)
items.text: State the four components of a time series.
items.model:
1. Trend (T): the long-term upward or downward movement.
2. Seasonal variation (S): regular, repeating patterns within a year (here, higher winter sweater demand).
3. Cyclical variation (C): longer, irregular swings around the trend, such as business cycles of more than a year.
4. Irregular/random variation (I): unpredictable one-off movements.

items.label: 3(b)(i)
items.text:
Monthly sweater demand, Ngundu Township shop (Jan to Dec), for 2022, 2023, 2024:
Jan 82, 85, 90; Feb 71, 85, 80; Mar 80, 93, 85; Apr 90, 95, 100; May 113, 125, 123; Jun 110, 115, 115; Jul 100, 102, 105; Aug 88, 102, 100; Sep 85, 90, 90; Oct 77, 78, 80; Nov 75, 72, 80; Dec 82, 78, 80.
Calculate the 3-point moving averages.

items.label: 3(b)(ii)
items.text: Calculate the 4-point moving averages.
items.model:
Because the question asks for seasonal indices by quarter, group the months into quarters (Jan–Mar, Apr–Jun, Jul–Sep, Oct–Dec). Quarterly totals for 2022–2024:
233, 313, 273, 234, 263, 335, 294, 228, 255, 338, 295, 240.
4-point moving averages: 263.25, 270.75, 276.25, 281.50, 280.00, 278.00, 278.75, 279.00, 282.00.
Centred 4-point averages (average of consecutive pairs, placed at Q3 2022 to Q2 2024): 267.00, 273.50, 278.88, 280.75, 279.00, 278.38, 278.88, 280.50.

items.label: 3(b)(iii)
items.text: Calculate the seasonal indices for each quarter.
items.model:
Ratio to centred average (quarterly total ÷ centred average):
Q3 = 1.0225, Q4 = 0.8556, Q1 = 0.9431, Q2 = 1.1932, Q3 = 1.0538, Q4 = 0.8190, Q1 = 0.9144, Q2 = 1.2050.
Average by quarter: Q1 = 0.9287, Q2 = 1.1991, Q3 = 1.0381, Q4 = 0.8373 (sum = 4.0033).
Adjust so the four indices average 1:  Q1 = 0.9280, Q2 = 1.1981, Q3 = 1.0373, Q4 = 0.8366.
April–June demand is highest (winter). October–December is the lowest.

items.label: 3(b)(iv)
items.text: Calculate the de-seasonalised values for the demand.

items.label: 3(b)(v)
items.text: Determine the trendline equation.
items.model:
Regress the de-seasonalised values on t = 1, 2, …, 12 (quarters).
Trend line: T = 259.72 + 2.38t.
Demand is rising by about 2.38 sweaters per quarter after removing seasonality.
items.teach: Least squares on the de-seasonalised series, not the raw data.

items.label: 4(a)(i)
items.text: Define: Critical region.
items.model: The set of values of the test statistic for which H0 is rejected. It has total probability α under H0.

items.label: 4(a)(ii)
items.text: Define: Type II error.
items.model: Failing to reject H0 when H0 is false. Its probability is β.

items.label: 4(a)(iii)
items.text: Define: Significance level.
items.model: The probability of rejecting H0 when it is true (Type I error), fixed in advance (α).

items.label: 4(a)(iv)
items.text: Define: The power of a statistical test.
items.model: The probability of correctly rejecting H0 when it is false: power = 1 − β.

items.label: 4(b)(i)
items.text:
A new drug is claimed to prevent sea sickness. A sample of 100 people on boat cruises:
               Sickness   No sickness
Drug taken        26          49
No drug taken     14          11
Use a χ² test at the 5% level to investigate whether there is evidence to support the claim.
items.model:
H0: sickness is independent of taking the drug. H1: they are associated.
Row totals 75 and 25; column totals 40 and 60; N = 100.
Expected: drug/sick = 75×40/100 = 30, drug/no sickness = 45, no drug/sick = 10, no drug/no sickness = 15.
χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 16/30 + 16/45 + 16/10 + 16/15 = 3.5556.
df = (2−1)(2−1) = 1. Critical χ²0.05,1 = 3.841.
Since 3.556 < 3.841, fail to reject H0.
items.teach: Expected counts come from row total × column total ÷ N.

items.label: 4(b)(ii)
items.text: State your conclusion clearly.
items.model: At the 5% level there is not enough evidence that the drug helps. Sickness was 34.7% (26/75) with the drug and 56.0% (14/25) without, but with these sample sizes the difference could be due to chance (p ≈ 0.059). A larger study is needed.

items.label: 5(a)(i)
items.text:
A life insurer tests a detailed screening form. Claim payments ($100 per year), normal:
With screening: 24.5, 21.7, 35.2, 15.9, 23.7, 34.2, 29.3, 21.1, 23.5, 28.3
Without screening: 22.4, 21.2, 36.3, 15.7, 21.5, 7.3, 12.8, 21.2, 23.9, 18.4
Calculate a 95% confidence interval for the difference between the mean claim amounts.

items.label: 5(a)(ii)
items.text: Comment on your answer.
items.model: The interval contains 0, so there is no significant difference between mean claims with and without screening at the 5% level. Screening has not been shown to reduce claims. The sample mean with screening is actually higher. The samples are small and the variances differ (36.2 against 58.4), so the pooled-variance assumption is questionable.

items.label: 5(b)(i)
items.text:
Monthly portfolio returns (%): Jan 5.0, Feb −1.9, Mar 9.7, Apr 6, May 2, Jun 0, Jul −4, Aug 3, Sep 0, Oct −2.3, Nov 5.6, Dec 7.0.
Calculate the target downside deviation when the target return is 4%.
items.model:
Keep only months below 4%: deviations (R − 4): Feb −5.9, May −2, Jun −4, Jul −8, Aug −1, Sep −4, Oct −6.3.
Squares: 34.81, 4, 16, 64, 1, 16, 39.69, sum = 175.50.
TDD = √[Σ(R − B)²/(n − 1)] = √(175.50/11) = 3.994%.
(Dividing by n = 12 instead gives 3.824%. State the convention used.)

items.label: 5(b)(ii)
items.text: Calculate the mean absolute deviation (MAD).

items.label: 5(c)
items.text: Outline the process for conducting simple random sampling.
items.model:
1. Define the target population and build a complete sampling frame (a list of all units).
2. Number every unit in the frame.
3. Decide the sample size n.
4. Select n numbers using a random number table or generator, so each unit has an equal chance.
5. Draw the units with those numbers (ignore repeats if sampling without replacement) and collect the data.

items.label: 5(d)(i)
items.text: What do you understand by: sampling frame?
items.model: The list or map of all units in the population from which the sample is drawn (e.g. a student register).

items.label: 5(d)(ii)
items.text: What do you understand by: sampling unit?
items.model: The individual element or group that can be selected for the sample (e.g. one student or one household).

items.label: 5(d)(iii)
items.text: What do you understand by: target population?
items.model: The entire group about which we want to draw conclusions.

items.label: 5(d)(iv)
items.text: What do you understand by: survey?
items.model: A method of collecting data from a sample (or the whole population) using questionnaires or interviews to learn about characteristics or opinions.

papers.title: Business Administration
papers.instructions: Time: 2½ hours. This paper carries five (5) questions. Answer ALL. Marks are indicated in brackets at the end of each question. Total marks are 100.

items.label: 1(a)
items.text: Discuss the roles played by managers in business organisations.
items.model:
Managers plan, organise, lead and control resources to achieve organisational goals. Mintzberg groups their roles in three sets:
• Interpersonal: figurehead (ceremonial duties), leader (motivating and directing staff), liaison (networking inside and outside the firm).
• Informational: monitor (scanning for information), disseminator (passing information to staff), spokesperson (representing the firm to outsiders).
• Decisional: entrepreneur (starting improvements and new ventures), disturbance handler (resolving crises and conflicts), resource allocator (budgets, people, time), negotiator (agreements with unions, suppliers, customers).
In practice a manager performs all of these every day, with the mix depending on the level of management.

items.label: 1(b)
items.text: Explain the difference between middle management and top management functions.
items.model:
Top management (board, CEO, directors) sets the vision, mission and long-term strategy. It makes policy and major investment decisions, deals with the external environment (government, shareholders, markets) and is accountable for overall performance. Its time horizon is long (3 to 5 years or more) and its decisions are strategic.
Middle management (department, divisional and branch managers) turns strategy into tactical plans. It coordinates departments, allocates resources to units, interprets policy for supervisors, monitors performance against targets and reports upward. Its time horizon is medium (about 1 year) and it is the link between top management and first-line supervisors.
In short: top management decides what the organisation will do and why. Middle management decides how each unit will do it.

items.text: Demonstrate the usefulness of Office Automation Systems in business administration activities.
items.model:
Office Automation Systems (OAS) use ICT to create, store, process and communicate office information. Examples are word processors, spreadsheets, e-mail, databases, calendars, video conferencing, scanners and document management systems.
Usefulness:
1. Speed and efficiency: documents, invoices and reports are produced and sent in minutes, with templates and mail merge.
2. Accuracy: spreadsheets and databases reduce arithmetic and copying errors in payroll, stock and accounts.
3. Communication and collaboration: e-mail, messaging and video meetings link staff, branches and customers, and support remote work.
4. Storage and retrieval: digital filing replaces paper, so records are found quickly and take little space.
5. Scheduling: shared calendars organise meetings, appointments and deadlines.
6. Decision support: summaries, charts and reports from data help managers decide.
7. Cost saving: less paper, printing, postage and clerical time.
8. Security and control: passwords, access rights and backups protect records.
9. Better customer service: faster responses and consistent documents.
Limitations to note: set-up and training costs, power and network dependence, and cyber risk, so firms need backups and security policies.

items.label: 3(a)
items.text: Discuss the methods used by organisations to ensure employee retention.
items.model:
1. Competitive pay and benefits: fair salaries, bonuses, medical aid, pension, housing or transport allowances.
2. Training and career development: skills training, study support, promotion paths and mentoring.
3. Recognition and rewards: praise, awards and performance incentives that make staff feel valued.
4. Good working conditions and work-life balance: safe workplace, reasonable hours, flexible working and leave.
5. Good leadership and communication: respectful supervisors, open feedback, and listening to staff.
6. Job enrichment and empowerment: meaningful tasks, autonomy and involvement in decisions.
7. Fair recruitment and induction: hiring people who fit the job and culture, then onboarding them well.
8. Job security and a positive culture: clear policies, fair treatment and teamwork.
9. Wellness programmes and exit interviews: support staff health and learn why people leave.

items.label: 3(b)(i)
items.text: Write short notes on: Franchise.
items.model: A franchise is a business arrangement where the franchisor grants the franchisee the right to use its brand, products and business system in return for fees and royalties. The franchisee operates the outlet independently (e.g. Pizza Inn, KFC outlets).

items.label: 3(b)(ii)
items.text: Write short notes on: Business Environment.
items.model: The business environment is all the internal and external factors that affect a firm's operations: the micro environment (customers, suppliers, competitors, employees) and the macro environment (political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors).

items.label: 3(b)(iii)
items.text: Write short notes on: Marketing Mix.
items.model: The marketing mix is the set of controllable tools a firm combines to reach its target market, the 4Ps: Product (quality, features, brand), Price (pricing strategy, discounts), Place (distribution and availability), Promotion (advertising, sales promotion, personal selling, PR). Service firms add People, Process and Physical evidence (7Ps).

items.text: Explain the McKinsey 7S model as a strategic planning tool in business and demonstrate its significance.
items.model:
The McKinsey 7S model (Peters and Waterman) says an organisation is effective only when seven interdependent elements are aligned.
Hard elements (easy to define and change):
• Strategy: the plan to gain competitive advantage.
• Structure: how the organisation is arranged (hierarchy, departments, reporting lines).
• Systems: the processes and procedures for daily work (IT, finance, HR systems).
Soft elements (harder to change, shaped by culture):
• Shared values: the core beliefs and purpose at the centre of the model.
• Skills: the capabilities of the organisation.
• Style: the leadership style and culture.
• Staff: the people, their numbers and development.
Significance:
1. It gives a holistic diagnosis, showing that strategy alone does not guarantee success.
2. It reveals misalignment (e.g. a new strategy with the wrong structure or skills).
3. It guides change management, mergers and restructuring.
4. It helps improve performance and align departments around shared values.
5. It is simple, and it can be used to plan future states by comparing the current and desired 7S positions.
Limitations: it is descriptive, gives no step-by-step method, and ignores the external environment.

items.text: The current business environment is faced with various business risks. Explain any five (5) causes of business risks and prescribe solutions.
items.model:
1. Economic instability (inflation, exchange rate swings, low demand): costs rise and sales fall. Solution: budgeting and regular price reviews, hedging or pricing in a stable currency, diversifying products and markets.
2. Technological and cyber risks (hacking, fraud, system failure, obsolete technology): data loss and downtime. Solution: firewalls, antivirus, backups, staff training, access controls, and a technology upgrade plan.
3. Competition and changing customer tastes: loss of market share. Solution: innovation, differentiation, quality and customer service, and market research.
4. Operational risks (power cuts, supply chain failure, equipment breakdown, human error): production stops. Solution: alternative power, more than one supplier, preventive maintenance, and clear procedures and training.
5. Legal, regulatory and political risks (policy changes, tax, licences, lawsuits): fines and disruption. Solution: compliance officers and audits, legal advice, keeping up with policy changes, and good contracts.
Also valid: financial risks (cash-flow problems, bad debts, solved by credit control and insurance) and natural disasters or pandemics (solved by insurance and a business continuity plan).
